By participating in COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, Ethiopia aims to forge partnerships, secure climate finance, and emphasize the continent's needs in global negotiations. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed highlighted the connection between climate action and economic policy, stressing that climate resilience is vital for Ethiopia's agricultural and hydropower-dependent economy. The country seeks to mobilize resources for renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, and climate-resilient infrastructure, while also promoting initiatives like the Africa Climate Innovation Compact. Ethiopia's hosting of COP32 is seen as a chance to strengthen Africa's negotiating position and showcase its potential as a leader in renewable energy solutions. The conference aims to shift the narrative from Africa as merely vulnerable to climate change to a continent rich in sustainable investment opportunities. Ethiopia's strategic approach emphasizes early action and accessible climate finance to bolster resilience and development. (158 words)

ethiopia.title: The Bone-Setters' Ward - How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia's Modern Healthcare Vacuum
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: The Bone-Setters' Ward - How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia's Modern Healthcare Vacuum - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: The Bone-Setters' Ward - How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia's Modern Healthcare Vacuum 13 November 2026 African Arguments analysis By Sleshi Teshome Kehali In a residential neighbourhood of Bahir Dar, in northwestern Ethiopia, patients visit the home of W/ro Birqe Yibre for help with injuries. Birqe, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, has practised for more than 20 years. One of her patients, Yidersal Mengistu, came with a painful right foot and a bruised big toe after kicking a stone while playing football. "I didn't go to the hospital. To be honest, I prefer the traditional way," Mengistu said. He explained that he had visited Birqe before for heel pain and believed her treatment had helped him. He also said she had treated him without charge on that earlier occasion. "If I recover fully this time, I will pay her," he said. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn For Birqe, payment depends partly on what patients can afford. She said people who have money typically pay between 150 and 200 Ethiopian birr, while she treats those who cannot pay without charging them. "If someone has no money, I treat them and tell them, 'Go on, go home,"' she said. "You cannot turn away poor people." A study of 836 people with a history of injury in Mecha district, published in BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies , found that 46.05 per cent had used traditional bone-setting services. Social acceptance was the most commonly reported reason for seeking this care. The findings reflect the study population in Mecha district and should not be taken as a national estimate. For patients such as Mengistu, the decision is also shaped by personal experience and trust. But the treatment of fractures and other serious injuries can carry risks when patients delay seeking medical assessment. Knowing When to Refer Birqe said she distinguishes between injuries she believes she can treat and those that require hospital care. "I handle muscle pulls and minor dislocations," she said. "If someone comes with a serious, displaced bone or a deep fracture, I tell them plainly to go to the hospital. I don't try to touch it." She said she was concerned about practitioners who accept serious cases despite lacking the necessary skills to manage them. According to Birqe, some bone-setters bind injured limbs tightly with bamboo splints, locally known as Timaq, and continue treatment even when a patient's condition worsens. She said some eventually advise patients to seek hospital care only after several visits. "When parents bring me a child whose hand is already ruined, I tell them: 'Run to the hospital, I won't touch this,"' she said. Her account highlights a distinction within traditional practice: while Birqe says she refers serious injuries, she believes other practitioners take on cases beyond their abilities. These claims describe her experience and observations; establishing how widespread such practices are would require further evidence. A Crooked Arm Thomas Habtamu, a student living in Bahir Dar, said a fall during a neighbourhood football match injured his left forearm. Because of his family's financial difficulties, he did not go to a hospital and instead sought treatment from a local Wogesha. "The healer kept massaging it week after week, telling me to be patient," Habtamu recalled. He said the injury was close to the joint and that the treatment did not restore the arm to its normal position. "He told me that if I ever fell down and hurt the arm again in the future, he might be able to reset it then," Habtamu said. Habtamu has never had the arm examined at a hospital. He said his forearm remains visibly bent and that he struggles with activities such as push-ups, lifting heavy objects and prolonged gym exercise. He contrasted his experience with that of a friend who sustained a similar injury around the same time. According to Habtamu, his friend went to hospital, underwent an operation in which a metal plate was inserted, and recovered the use of his arm within about two months. The two accounts illustrate the different experiences the men reported. Without medical records or an examination, however, the precise nature of Habtamu's injury and the extent to which the treatment contributed to his current condition remain unconfirmed. What Happens When Fractures Are Not Properly Treated? At Tibebe Ghion Specialized Hospital in Bahir Dar, Dr Biruk Ferede, an orthopaedic specialist, said some patient's mistake natural bone healing for proof that a traditional treatment has worked. "An undisplaced fracture can heal naturally on its own; bone is living tissue that knits over time," he said. He warned that manipulating a displaced fracture or an injured joint without appropriate assessment can cause further problems. One possible complication is malunion, in which a fractured bone heals in an incorrect position. Dr. Biruk said correcting such injuries can require more complex surgery than treating them soon after they occur. He explained that surgeons may need to cut and realign a bone that has healed in the wrong position and secure it with plates. Stiffness in a nearby joint can make treatment more difficult, particularly when care has been delayed. Dr. Biruk also raised concerns about tightly applied traditional splints, especially when used on children. Swelling around an injured limb can increase pressure beneath a tight binding and compromise blood circulation. Severe cases may result in permanent tissue damage. He said children are particularly vulnerable because they may be unable to communicate the severity of their pain or remove a restrictive splint themselves. "Children cry continuously, but parents may assume the crying is just normal pain," he said. He described cases in which children arrived at hospital with severely damaged limbs and amputation was considered necessary. Trust, Access and Medical Care Dr. Biruk said social expectations can also influence treatment decisions. He recalled an incident involving a fifth-year medical student who sustained a fracture. According to the doctor, family members and neighbours took the student to a Wogesha before the student could decide where to seek care. "If an educated medical student faces that kind of pressure, what do you expect from ordinary citizens?" he asked. The incident, as recounted by Dr. Biruk, illustrates the influence that family and community expectations can have on decisions about treatment. It does not establish how frequently this happens, but it offers an example of how social pressure may affect an individual's choices even when formal medical care is familiar to them. Some health advocates have suggested providing traditional bone-setters with basic training to help them recognise serious injuries and refer patients to hospitals. Dr. Biruk is sceptical that short training can make practitioners safe to manage fractures. "Becoming an orthopaedic surgeon requires years of medical education and specialist training," he said. "You cannot turn someone into a safe trauma practitioner with short training." He argued that basic first-aid awareness should be available to the public, while suspected fractures and serious injuries should receive assessment from qualified medical professionals. Birqe's account, meanwhile, points to why some patients continue to seek help outside hospitals: she offers familiar care and says she does not turn away people who cannot pay. Habtamu's experience shows why a patient's decision about where to seek treatment can have lasting consequences. Their stories do not establish that all traditional bone-setters practise in the same way, or that every patient who visits one will suffer complications. They do, however, raise questions about how people assess injuries, what influences their choices and how quickly they can access appropriate medical care. For patients with suspected fractures, the challenge is to seek treatment that addresses the injury before complications develop. Understanding why people turn to traditional practitioners is part of that challenge, but so is ensuring that serious injuries receive timely medical attention. Research published in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery examined amputations associated with traditional bone-setting in southern Ethiopia. During an initial two-year retrospective review, researchers recorded 49 amputations, 25 of which were associated with gangrene following tight splintage by traditional bone-setters. After instructional courses were provided to 112 traditional healers and local health assistants, a subsequent two-year prospective study recorded 25 amputations, including seven associated with gangrene. The author concluded that educating traditional healers could help reduce amputations caused by gangrene. However, the findings come from a specific setting and period and should not be treated as a measure of the prevalence of these complications across Ethiopia. Opinion November 15, 2026 Updated: November 15, 2026 Beyond the Battlefield: Zemene Kassie’s Reported Conversation with the UN Special Envoy and the Changing Political Dynamics of Ethiopia November 15, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Political Legitimacy, International Engagement, the Alliance for Survival, and the Future of Conflict Resolution in the Horn of Africa Caleb Ta (Dr.) Independent Researcher in African Political Affairs & Human Rights Advocate Beyond What Is Visible In politics, the most consequential developments are not always the most visible. A single conversation may appear insignificant on the surface, yet beneath it may lie shifting political calculations, emerging alliances, competing interests, and changing perceptions of power. What is visible may be only the beginning of a much larger story. The reported telephone conversation between Zemene Kassie, Chairman of the Amhara Fano National Movement and a leading figure in the Alliance for Survival (Tibebir Lehelwuna), and Ambassador Guang Cong, the United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, deserves serious political and diplomatic attention. Its significance extends beyond the immediate exchange between two individuals. It raises fundamental questions about political legitimacy, international engagement, the changing balance of political power in Ethiopia, and the future of conflict resolution in the Horn of Africa. Although a telephone conversation does not constitute formal recognition or diplomatic endorsement, it can carry considerable political significance. In a country where the government has sought to portray armed opposition movements as isolated security threats, direct engagement by a senior United Nations representative introduces an important dimension into the political equation: the possibility that Ethiopia’s internal conflicts must be addressed through engagement with the actual political and military actors involved, rather than through a government-defined security narrative alone. The importance of this development should therefore be assessed through three interconnected lenses: the changing political status of the Amhara movement, the internationalization of Ethiopia’s internal political crisis, and the broader implications for regional stability. From a Domestic Security Narrative to an International Political Question For several years, the Ethiopian government’s approach to the Amhara conflict has largely been framed through the language of law enforcement, counterinsurgency, and national security. The government has repeatedly characterized Fano and associated movements through labels such as rebels, extremists, criminals, and destabilizing forces. This political framing has significant consequences. When an internal conflict is presented exclusively as a law-enforcement matter, the possibility of addressing its underlying political grievances becomes substantially restricted. It also creates an environment in which military solutions are presented as the principal, sometimes exclusive, means of resolving the crisis. However, the persistence of armed conflict raises a fundamental question: Can a government achieve sustainable peace by treating a politically significant and geographically established armed movement exclusively as a security problem? The reported engagement between Ambassador Guang Cong and Zemene Kassie challenges the assumption that the Ethiopian conflict can be understood without hearing directly from the actors involved.It suggests an important diplomatic principle: sustainable conflict resolution requires an understanding of the political realities on the ground, including the grievances, objectives, organizational structures, and positions of parties involved in the conflict. This is not equivalent to endorsing an armed movement. It is an acknowledgment of the practical requirements of conflict prevention and political mediation. In conflict diplomacy, the distinction between recognizing an actor as an interlocutor and recognizing it as a legitimate government is fundamental. International representatives routinely communicate with parties to conflicts without conferring statehood, government authority, or political endorsement upon them. Nevertheless, the willingness to establish direct communication can represent a meaningful change in diplomatic engagement. The Transformation from a ‘Rebel Leader’ Narrative to a Political Interlocutor Perhaps the most consequential aspect of this development concerns the politics of labeling. Political conflicts are not fought exclusively through military force. They are also fought through narratives, terminology, diplomatic representation, and the ability to define who constitutes a legitimate participant in political discussions. For years, the Ethiopian government’s public narrative has sought to categorize Fano leadership as a collection of criminal or insurgent actors rather than as representatives of a broader political movement with articulated grievances and objectives. The significance of the reported conversation lies partly in the fact that an international diplomatic representative has engaged directly with one of the movement’s prominent leaders. In diplomatic terminology, such a person can be described as an interlocutor: someone with whom an international representative communicates to understand political positions, explore possible solutions, and assess opportunities for dialogue. This distinction matters. An actor that is consistently excluded from political engagement may find it difficult to have its grievances incorporated into an internationally supported peace process. Conversely, direct communication creates an opportunity for its positions to be heard and evaluated independently. What it does demonstrate, if the reported account is accurate, is a willingness to engage with a significant Ethiopian political and armed actor. That is a meaningful development in itself. The Alliance for Survival and the Question of Ethiopia’s Political Reality Another important dimension is the political significance of the Alliance for Survival. According to the movement’s stated position, the alliance brings together Ethiopian forces with shared political interests and concerns about their collective future. Its proponents describe it as an Ethiopian political coalition rather than an externally controlled project or a separatist undertaking. This distinction deserves serious consideration.The existence of multiple political and armed actors within Ethiopia demonstrates that the country’s political landscape cannot be reduced to the relationship between the federal government and a single opposition organization. Ethiopia’s crisis involves competing political interests, questions of representation, unresolved historical grievances, regional tensions, and disputes over the distribution and exercise of state power. The emergence of broader political cooperation among different forces potentially introduces another dimension into this environment.It also raises an important question for international diplomacy: Can a sustainable political settlement be achieved without understanding the objectives and positions of the different actors who have the capacity to influence the country’s security and political future? The answer is difficult to avoid.Any serious peace initiative must take account of the actors whose participation is necessary for ending hostilities and implementing a settlement. The Alliance for Survival therefore has an opportunity to demonstrate that its political objectives extend beyond military confrontation. It must articulate a credible political program, establish transparent organizational structures, demonstrate respect for civilian protection and human rights, and explain how it envisions an inclusive political transition. Its credibility will ultimately depend not simply on its ability to attract diplomatic attention, but on the political principles and conduct it demonstrates. Ethiopia’s Internal Conflict Cannot Be Separated from the Security of the Horn of Africa The broader regional context makes this diplomatic development particularly significant. Ethiopia occupies a strategically important position in the Horn of Africa. Its political stability is interconnected with developments in Sudan, South Sudan, Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti, and the wider Red Sea region. Instability in Ethiopia has consequences beyond its borders. Likewise, tensions among neighboring countries can intensify existing domestic political and security challenges. The region is characterized by interconnected security concerns, including cross-border armed movements, displacement, refugee flows, competing geopolitical interests, contested borders, and struggles over strategic economic corridors. These challenges cannot be understood independently. Ambassador Guang Cong’s diplomatic responsibilities are particularly relevant in this regard. The United Nations appointed him Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa in July 2025. His professional experience includes extensive involvement in peace operations in Sudan, Darfur, and South Sudan. His regional engagement has also reflected the interconnected nature of security challenges across Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan, Somalia, South Sudan, and the Red Sea. On October 29, 2026, he convened a regional diplomatic retreat in Nairobi, bringing together special envoys, ambassadors, regional organizations, and international partners to discuss peace and security developments across the Horn. Consequently, the reported conversation with Zemene Kassie should be examined within the wider diplomatic effort to understand and address the region’s interconnected conflicts. The critical issue is that Ethiopia’s internal political crisis cannot be resolved simply by examining the country’s relationships with Sudan and Eritrea. Nor can regional stability be achieved by ignoring the political grievances and conflicts developing inside Ethiopia. Both dimensions matter. 5. The Diplomatic Dilemma for Addis Ababa One of the most important developments in this situation is the contrast between the government’s diplomatic narrative and the possibility of direct international engagement with domestic opposition actors. On November 11, 2026, Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on East African affairs, met Ambassador Guang Cong. According to Getachew’s public account, their discussions addressed the conflicts in Sudan and Somalia and what he described as the destabilizing role of Eritrea in the region. He also alleged that Eritrean and Sudanese leaders were supporting, arming, and coordinating armed elements operating inside Ethiopia. These are serious allegations and should be independently investigated rather than automatically accepted or dismissed.Nevertheless, the diplomatic contrast is significant. The Ethiopian government’s position emphasizes the alleged external sponsorship of domestic armed opposition. The reported conversation with Zemene Kassie, meanwhile, introduces the perspective of an internal Ethiopian political and armed actor directly into the diplomatic discussion. This creates an important analytical distinction. If Ethiopia’s conflict is understood primarily as a product of external interference, the proposed solution will naturally emphasize diplomatic pressure on neighboring governments and the interruption of external support. But if the conflict is also understood as the product of unresolved domestic political grievances, competing claims to political representation, and contested state authority, then the solution must include an internal political process. These approaches are not necessarily mutually exclusive. External interference, if established, must be addressed. However, external factors cannot substitute for an honest examination of domestic political causes. The fundamental question is whether the Ethiopian government is prepared to acknowledge that sustainable peace requires political engagement with domestic opponents, rather than relying exclusively on military operations and accusations against neighboring countries. Moving Beyond the Battlefield to the Diplomatic Arena: A Potential Change in Political Status One of the most significant implications of the reported conversation between Zemene Kassie and Ambassador Guang Cong is the possibility that the Amhara movement is beginning to move beyond the battlefield and into the international diplomatic arena. For a political movement engaged in an armed struggle, direct communication with a United Nations Special Envoy can represent an important development in how its political position, objectives, and grievances are communicated internationally. It creates an opportunity to present its perspective directly to an international diplomatic representative and to bring issues that have largely been discussed within Ethiopia’s domestic conflict into a broader international political conversation. Political movements are not measured exclusively by their military capabilities. Their long-term political significance also depends on their ability to articulate their objectives, communicate with international institutions, establish diplomatic relationships, and present credible political alternatives. In this context, the reported conversation may indicate an emerging change in the movement’s political and diplomatic standing. Rather than being discussed exclusively as a force operating on the battlefield, the movement has an opportunity to present itself as a political actor whose grievances, objectives, and participation may need to be considered in efforts to resolve Ethiopia’s conflict. This distinction is important. Direct diplomatic engagement does not automatically constitute formal recognition or endorsement by the United Nations. Nevertheless, it can create an important channel of communication, increase international awareness, and open possibilities for further diplomatic engagement. In conflicts where military confrontation has failed to produce a sustainable resolution, such communication can become an important first step toward political dialogue. The significance, therefore, lies in the possibility of a transition from military visibility to diplomatic engagement—from being known primarily through the dynamics of armed confrontation to having an opportunity to articulate political demands within an international forum. Engagement with the UN Special Envoy also provides an opportunity to communicate concerns about civilian protection, human rights, territorial disputes, political representation, and the future of Ethiopia’s political arrangements. These are not merely military questions; they are political issues that require diplomatic attention and, ultimately, a negotiated resolution. What This Could Mean for the Future of the Movement The movement now faces an important opportunity: translating diplomatic contact into a coherent, credible, and sustained international engagement strategy. A single telephone conversation, however significant, cannot by itself establish lasting diplomatic influence. Its importance will ultimately depend on what follows: whether communication continues, whether substantive political issues receive further attention, and whether the movement demonstrates the political maturity and organizational capacity necessary to participate constructively in a broader peace process. Several priorities deserve particular attention: Political representation: Clearly communicate the movement’s political objectives, organizational structure, and the interests of the communities it seeks to represent. Its international engagement should explain not only what it opposes but also what political future it proposes. Civilian protection: Place the protection of civilians, respect for human rights, and unhindered humanitarian access at the center of its international engagement. The protection of civilian life must remain a fundamental responsibility, regardless of the circumstances of the conflict. International accountability: Encourage impartial, independent investigations into alleged human rights violations and atrocities committed by all parties to the conflict. Credible accountability requires evidence, transparency, and equal application of international standards. Political credibility: Develop and communicate a transparent political vision grounded in democratic governance, equality, constitutional rights, political representation, and the protection of all Ethiopian communities. Commitment to political dialogue: Demonstrate readiness to participate in meaningful, inclusive negotiations aimed at addressing the underlying causes of the conflict and establishing a sustainable political settlement. These priorities would help transform diplomatic contact into meaningful political engagement. They would also strengthen the movement’s ability to communicate with international institutions as a political actor capable of articulating a coherent agenda and contributing to a negotiated solution. Ultimately, the reported telephone conversation between Zemene Kassie and Guang Cong should be viewed as a potentially significant diplomatic development for the Amhara movement. It signals an opportunity to move beyond a predominantly domestic conflict narrative and place political grievances, territorial questions, human rights concerns, and demands for political representation within a broader international discussion. The central question is no longer simply how the movement is positioned on the battlefield, but whether it can translate its political influence into meaningful diplomatic engagement and a recognized place in discussions about Ethiopia’s political future. That is the potential change of status: a movement seeking to move from the battlefield into the diplomatic arena, from military confrontation toward political engagement, and from being discussed by international actors to having an opportunity to communicate directly with them. The International Community Must Move Beyond Symbolic Engagement While the reported conversation represents a potentially important opening, its long-term significance will depend on what follows.Diplomatic contact alone cannot end a conflict that has developed through years of mistrust, violence, political exclusion, and competing claims to authority. The United Nations and other international partners should therefore consider several practical measures. First, they should support an inclusive political dialogue that incorporates the relevant Ethiopian political stakeholders, including representatives of the Amhara community and other conflict-affected populations. Second, allegations of mass atrocities, ethnic targeting, unlawful killings, displacement, and other serious human rights violations must receive independent, impartial, and credible investiga
ethiopia.summary: The reported conversation between Zemene Kassie, Chairman of the Amhara Fano National Movement, and Ambassador Guang Cong, the UN Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, highlights shifting political dynamics in Ethiopia. This engagement suggests a potential re-evaluation of how the Ethiopian government addresses its internal conflicts, particularly regarding the Amhara movement, which has been framed as a security threat. The conversation underscores the importance of recognizing political grievances and the necessity of including various actors in conflict resolution efforts. It challenges the narrative that armed movements can be solely treated as security issues, advocating for a more nuanced understanding of Ethiopia's political landscape. The Alliance for Survival, which Kassie represents, aims to unify various Ethiopian forces with shared interests, emphasizing the need for a credible political program. This development is significant not only for Ethiopia but also for regional stability in the Horn of Africa, where interconnected security challenges persist.

Government leaders, opposition parties, armed actors, and civil-society institutions may all prefer a peaceful, prosperous country to protracted confrontation. But they do not. The application of this or any other theory to unbundle Ethiopia’s deeply rooted problems require s moral and spiritual anchors. When we unbundle, we must try to understand the political cultures and behaviors of political elites in Ethiopia. Why did they form political movements like the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Party (EPRP. the All-Ethiopian Socialist Movement (MEISONE, the Coalition for Unity and Democracy (CUD). Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA), Coalition of Ethiopian Democratic Force, Hibr Ethiopia and more that collapsed? This requires more in-depth research and analysis. What is the missing link? Is it cultural? Is it moral? Is it spiritual? Is it psychological? Is it greed? Is it individualism and individual ego? Is it lack critical thinking? Is it lust for power? Cooperation is far better and essential for mutual survival than recurrent fighting that entails deaths and destruction. All Ethiopians deserve recognition that they are human and share the same needs—dignity and human warmth, peace, stability, fair treatment, food, drinkable or clean water, sanitation, health, education, and shelter. This can only happen through cooperation and not through self serring initiatives and single ethnic elite hegemony. The magnitude of the problem must inform what we do and what we demand. Yet each actor or contestant tends to believe that yielding first will invite repression, exclusion, territorial loss, or humiliation. There is a persistent trust gap. When commitments are not credible, confrontation becomes individually defensible even though cooperation would make society better off. The policy task is therefore not to preach consensus; it is to redesign the strategic environment in which leaders and civil society make choices. Ethiopian society cannot afford to continue with the same paradigm of thinking as the conflict ridden past. The analysis is a diagnostic model, a tool. It is not a claim that all actors are equally powerful, culpable, or motivated. The state carries special legal and practical obligations regarding protection, rights, public administration, and its use of coercive power. Sadly, for Ethiopia, the state is no longer impartial. In many respects, it is prone to terrorism. It deploys drones and slaughters school children and the rest every week. Ethiopia’s 140 million people, more than 60 percent multidimensionally poor, are incapacitated. Civil society cannot substitute for armed-party security guarantees; and victims’ rights cannot be traded away for a superficial bargain. For this commentary, the Nash Equilibrium model comes in handy. Who is Nash? Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive. John F. Nash Jr. Winner of Sverige’s Riksbank Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1994. He was affiliated with Princeton. He won this prize for his pioneering analysis of equilibria in the theory of non-cooperative games. This analysis is pertinent to my commentary. The Road Map proposal I posted on November 9, 2026, is only feasible if Ethiopian moves from a fighting mode to a cooperative one. 1 | The Nash equilibrium: why a bad outcome persists. A Nash equilibrium is a situation in which no actor can improve its expected payoff by changing strategy alone while everyone else keeps theirs unchanged. In other words, the Prosperity Party’s model of a zero-sum game engenders more inequality, human suffering, war, and instability. Consider two broad strategic blocs: (A) incumbent authorities and allied institutions; and (B) opposition and other organized challengers. Each chooses credible cooperation (C) or defensive domination/obstruction (D). The illustrative payoffs below are ordinal, not measurements of Ethiopia; higher numbers signify more preferred outcomes for that actor. Authority / challenger Challenger cooperates (C) Challenger defects (D) Authority cooperates (C) (4, 4) shared gains (1, 5) exposed authority Authority defects (D) (5, 1) exposed challenger (2, 2) costly standoff Here D strictly dominates C for each bloc: if the other cooperates, opportunistic defection yields five rather than four; if the other defects, defensive defection yields two rather than one. Thus (D, D) is the Nash equilibrium even though (C, C) being collectively superior. This is a Prisoner’s Dilemma representation—not a finding that every Ethiopian actor has precisely these preferences. Some interactions instead resemble a “stag hunt,” in which cooperation is also an equilibrium but fragile because each party doubts the other will cooperate. Mutual mistrust exists in this case. 2 | What makes the Ethiopian trap durable? Institutional commitment failures. Ethiopia’s national institutions are gutted. Governance is characterized by weakly trusted enforcement, disputed rules of competition, contested federal–regional authorities and uncertainty over security arrangements that make these promises reversible. Winners fear future retaliation; losers fear permanent exclusion. Structural asymmetry Control of security forces, administrative resources, public media, and fiscal transfers is unequal. Symmetric moral appeals therefore miss asymmetric responsibilities. Some opposition groups also possess coercive capacity that requires specific ceasefire and disarmament arrangements. It is matter of sheer survival. Psychological and historical mechanisms. Collective trauma, fear of domination, identity-based threat perceptions, humiliation, zero-sum narratives, and reciprocal attribution of bad faith narrow the set of politically imaginable compromises. Spoilers and audience costs. Moderates may be punished by hard-liners for compromise; leaders risk reputational loss when concessions are interpreted as surrender. Diaspora narratives, misinformation, and conflict entrepreneurs can increase the apparent payoff to defection. Lack of credible sequence. The chicken or the egg syndrome. “Disarm first,” “reform first,” or “trust us first” are often impossible demands when implementation is irreversible for one side and reversible for the other. It is hard to disarm when the state that commands superior military force is out there to kill you. 3 | Change the payoffs, not just the rhetoric. Ethiopian elites talk about transition constantly. The transition strategy should make the expected reward from verified cooperation exceed the reward from opportunistic defection. In simplified terms, cooperate when the expected gains from inclusion, protection, and reconstruction—plus the value of future cooperation—outweigh the perceived security risks and domestic political penalties of compromise. Make promises observable (transparent) Publish clear commitments, dates, and responsible institutions. Use independently verified ceasefire/civilian-protection reporting, accessible complaint channels, and regular public progress dashboards. Where feasible, include neutral African Union–supported verification and local monitors with protection against retaliation. Make cooperation reciprocal but not hostage to perfect trust. Stage limited, simultaneous and verifiable moves: cease attacks and protect access; release agreed categories of detainees after due process review; restore services and communications; expand lawful civic space; negotiate remaining security matters. Each step unlocks the next without making civilians bargaining chips. Protect legitimate political loss. Create minimum guarantees for peaceful opposition, media, civil society, and regional participation—including judicial remedies and enforceable safeguards against collective punishment. Political competition must become survivable for losers, not a contest for existential control. Reduce the gain from defection Attach transparent, lawful consequences to renewed attacks, intimidation, and obstruction; preserve independent investigations and remedies for serious abuses. Never offer blanket impunity for grave crimes. Incentives should distinguish political reintegration from criminal accountability. ACCOUNTABILITY IS CRITICAL IN ALL CASES PAST OR CURRENT. You cannot afford to ignore a Mai Kadra like massacre repeated across ethnic and faith groups throughout the country without accountability for war crimes, crimes of genocide and ethnic cleansing. Change social expectations Support cross-community deliberation, trauma-sensitive listening, joint public-service projects, and leaders’ repeated messages recognizing each group’s fears without validating attacks. Independent civic actors should monitor fairness rather than simply endorse a preselected settlement. Social and political actors must put a timeline concerning the steps they intend to take and implement them diligently. 4 | Apply the model to the existing four-phase roadmap (to follow) Phase I — 0–6 months: protect civilians and stabilize. Secure localized cessation arrangements, humanitarian corridors, essential services, and independent civilian-protection monitoring. Establish an incident-reporting and rapid dispute-resolution mechanism. Strategic effect: lower the immediate fear-based payoff from preemptive violence. Phase II — 6–18 months: negotiate and verify guarantees. Publish the National Dialogue recommendations alongside an itemized government response; create inclusive, independently facilitated negotiations on security, political participation, interim local administration, detainees, land/property disputes, and reintegration. Allow meaningful dissent and supplementary processes for those absent from the prior dialogue. Strategic effect: make cooperation credible and political exclusion less likely. Phase III — 1–3 years: reconstruct services and institutions. Restore schools, clinics, water, agriculture, and roads through independently reviewed criteria; strengthen courts, financial controls, and local administrations; create survivor-centered truth, remedy, and accountability pathways. Strategic effect: deliver visible dividends to cooperation and restore neutral state capacity. Phase IV — 3–10 years: consolidate accountable peace. Institutionalize lawful, competitive politics, fair fiscal federalism, oversight, dispute resolution, rights protection, and broad-based jobs, with annual independent audits and course corrections. Strategic effect: make future cooperation self-enforcing through repeated interaction and predictable institutions. These phases overlap; progress is conditional on evidence, not the calendar. Do not wait for a complete constitutional settlement before protecting civilians, and do not confuse a ceasefire with a durable political settlement. Convene a bounded “non-domination and mutual-security compact” among federal and regional authorities, relevant armed and non-armed political actors, independent civil-society representatives, women’s groups, displaced persons, and survivor organizations. Facilitation should be accepted by the parties, with African Union support in cases where it is useful. The initial mandate should be narrow: protection, access, verification, political inclusion, and an agreed timetable—not immediate consensus on every constitutional question. A compact or charter becomes credible only when each side can answer four questions: What exactly must I do? Who verifies the other side? What protects me if the other side breaches? What lawful, proportional remedy follows noncompliance? Publish those answers in understandable language and in relevant local languages. Suggested monitoring scorecard Indicator Evidence to publish Civilian protection Verified incidents, access, and response times by area Political space Arbitrary detention complaints resolved; permitted peaceful activity Dialogue inclusion Stakeholder participation, dissenting views and written responses Delivery of guarantees Milestones met/late with independent confirmation Public trust Repeat anonymous surveys disaggregated by region and community 6 | Limits and critical safeguards Game theory clarifies incentives but cannot reduce Ethiopian history, federalism, identities, and grievances to a two-player contest. Actors are heterogeneous; preferences shift; violence is not morally symmetrical; and external parties can alter incentives. The model must therefore be assessed against field evidence, revised after each phase, and accompanied by constitutional, historical, human-rights and political-economy analysis. A settlement that rewards violence while silencing peaceful civic participation may merely create another unstable equilibrium. Conclusion Ethiopia does not lack appeals for unity. It lacks sufficiently trusted institutions and arrangements through which political rivals can cooperate without fearing annihilation or permanent subordination. The road out is a verified sequence of civilian protection, mutually enforceable guarantees, visible reconstruction benefits, and rules that let every community and party compete peacefully without seeking hegemony. it behooves us to ask ourselves “Who is the real enemy” of the Ethiopian people? Are we part of the problem or part of the solution? I do not know the answer. But at least we can cooperate with one another in search of answers, the truth. The decisive question is not “Who will compromise first?” but “What guarantees make it rational for each to cooperate now?” It is the commonality Ethiopians share and deserve as human beings and citizens that dictates cooperation rather than constant friction and confrontation. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's ongoing political crisis is characterized by a self-reinforcing non-cooperative equilibrium, where various actors—government leaders, opposition parties, and civil society—prefer peace but remain entrenched in conflict. This situation is analyzed through the lens of Nash equilibrium, illustrating how mutual mistrust leads to a costly standoff rather than cooperation. The article emphasizes that Ethiopia's political culture is marred by historical grievances, fear of domination, and a lack of credible commitments, which perpetuates the cycle of violence and instability. To break this cycle, the author proposes a four-phase roadmap focused on cooperation, accountability, and rebuilding trust among stakeholders. Key steps include protecting civilians, negotiating guarantees, reconstructing services, and institutionalizing accountable governance. The article argues that without a shift from a zero-sum mentality to a cooperative framework, Ethiopia's path to peace and stability will remain obstructed, necessitating a fundamental change in the strategic environment that influences political choices.

ethiopia.content: KDF team detonates three RPG explosives near Kenya-Ethiopia border amid crisis - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY KDF team detonates three RPG explosives near Kenya-Ethiopia border amid crisis Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ by CYRUS OMBATI Friday November 13, 2026 IG Kanja in Moyale A team of Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) personnel safely detonated three rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs) discovered near the Kenya-Ethiopia border in the Sessi area of Moyale, Marsabit County. The detonation was the second exercise in two weeks, officials said amid a growing crisis. The explosives, which had no visible registration markings, were destroyed on Monday, November 9, following reports that two RPGs had landed near a slaughter site close to the border. The two explosives, fitted with stabilising fins at the rear, were reportedly fired from Ethiopia at around 2 am Monday before landing a few metres inside Kenyan territory, officials said. KDF officers based in Moyale carried out the controlled demolition, with no injuries or property damage reported. advertisements On their way back from the demolition site, the soldiers discovered a third RPG along the roadside near Sessi Mixed Secondary School. The third explosive, which did not have stabilising fins, was also safely detonated. Authorities said they had increased security personnel in the area to address the growing crisis. The explosives are being launched by rival groups targeting those seeking refuge in Kenyan side. The government has confirmed that approximately 40,000 Ethiopians have crossed into Kenya and are currently being hosted in Moyale following escalating tensions in parts of Ethiopia. Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said tensions in Ethiopia had forced thousands of people to flee into Kenya. "The issue is that from the Ethiopian side, they have been having a little bit of tension over there. So, the problem has caused about 40,000 people to evacuate to Kenya," he said. Mudavadi said he had communicated with his Ethiopian counterpart and asked him to intervene and help stabilise the situation so that the displaced families can return home. "I told him to try and calm the situation in their country so that the refugees return to their homes," he said. He added that the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it was working to restore normalcy. "They have assured us that they will do their best to return the issues to normalcy and then the people can go back," Mudavadi said. The displacement follows clashes that erupted in October 2026, amid longstanding disagreements between the Oromia and Somali regional administrations over territorial boundaries and administrative control. The fighting has displaced thousands of people, with many families seeking shelter in schools, churches and temporary camps, while others have been accommodated by relatives and members of the local community. Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja ordered the deployment of additional police officers to Moyale, Marsabit County, amid growing security concerns linked to developments in neighbouring Ethiopia. Kanja announced the reinforcement on November 5, during a security assessment visit to the border town, where he chaired a strategic meeting with regional security commanders to review the prevailing security situation. He directed officers deployed in the area to remain on high alert and strengthen surveillance to protect residents and their property. The Inspector General assured residents that the National Police Service (NPS) was committed to maintaining peace and stability in the region through enhanced security operations. “We are here to ensure all the visitors and locals are safe. We will ensure more personnel arrive for protection,” he said. He also urged members of the public to cooperate with security agencies by providing timely and relevant information that could help prevent security threats. Kanja toured a camp hosting families displaced by insecurity, where he assured them of enhanced protection and coordinated humanitarian assistance in partnership with relief agencies. The security assessment comes amid concerns over instability in neighbouring Ethiopia and its potential implications for security along Kenya's northern border. Kanja was accompanied by Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) Director Mohammed Amin, General Service Unit (GSU) Commandant Johanna Tonui and Kenya Police Service Director of Operations Philip Opiyo. Others present included Eastern Regional Commissioner Jacob Muganda, Eastern Regional Police Commander Stephen Chebet, Eastern Regional Administration Police Commander Michael Owino and Regional Criminal Investigations Officer Michael Sang, alongside other senior security officials. The visit came a day after a 20-year-old woman was seriously injured after being struck by two suspected stray bullets believed to have originated from neighbouring Ethiopia in Moyale, Marsabit County. The incident occurred on November 4, 2026, at approximately 12:15pm while the victim was at her home in Biashara area. Police said she was hit by two bullets in the back, leaving her unconscious. She was rushed to Taqwa Nursing Home Hospital, where medical personnel removed the two bullets. The victim was admitted in serious condition as police documented the incident. The circumstances under which the bullets crossed into Kenyan territory remain unclear. This is the latest such incident in the area amid growing crisis due to ongoing fighting in Ethiopia pitting two communities. A 65-year-old woman was killed in the area, after she was reportedly struck by a suspected stray bullet believed to have originated from ongoing clashes in neighbouring Ethiopia. The deceased was identified as Amina Guchi, who was reportedly at the Moyale County offices, located next to Moyale Law Courts, when the incident occurred on November 2, 2026. Guchi was speaking to a security official on duty when an object believed to be a stray bullet struck her on the head from behind. She collapsed and lost consciousness before being rushed to Moyale Sub-County Referral Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival. Police officers subsequently visited the hospital, where a post-mortem examination was conducted before the body was released to the family for burial arrangements. The neighbouring Moyale is experiencing conflict which has displaced more than 50,000 people. Security officers in the area had earlier on safely detonated three rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs) that reportedly landed in the area after being discharged from neighbouring Ethiopia. The explosives were discovered on Sunday, November 1, 2026, following a report about unexploded explosive materials that had landed near Sessi Primary School. This affected learning and examinations at the centre. Two Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examination centres in Moyale Sub-County, Marsabit County, were relocated following the insecurity linked to clan clashes along the Kenya-Ethiopia border. According to police, the explosives were found at two locations- one at Sessi Primary School and two others at the Meteorological Department offices. Police and a team of bomb disposal experts from the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) based at Odha rushed to the scene. The security team established that the materials were three RPGs, which were subsequently secured, removed and safely detonated by the bomb experts. At least three people had been injured after bullets hit structures in the area two weeks ago. The United Nations refugee agency has warned of growing humanitarian needs in northern Kenya after an estimated 50,000 people fled clashes in Ethiopia and crossed the border into Moyale in search of safety. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said significant cross-border movements had been reported since October 22, with the number of arrivals remaining fluid as registration and verification efforts continued. Local authorities estimate that up to 50,000 people have entered Kenya, with reports indicating that additional crossings could further increase the number of people requiring assistance. Many of those fleeing the violence are women and children, raising concerns over their protection and access to essential services. The conflict started three weeks ago following the alleged raising of the flag of the Somali Regional State in Ethiopia, which triggered clashes between forces and groups from the Oromia and Somali regional states. According to UNHCR, some arrivals are staying with relatives and host communities, while others have sought temporary shelter in schools and churches. EST to November 13 at 9:00 A.M. EST. To receive the Africa File, Ethiopia War Security Review, or Congo War Security Review via email, please subscribe here . Follow CTP on X , LinkedIn , and BlueSky for daily updates. Read CTP’s latest analysis on the war in Ethiopia in the weekly Africa File here . Key Takeaways: Northern Axis. Local sources claimed that Amhara Fano National Movement fighters fought alongside Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) forces against Ethiopian federal forces near the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, although the Critical Threats Project (CTP) could not confirm the unverified claims. Western Axis. The Ethiopian military reportedly sustained fighting with TPLF and Eritrean forces around Badme, an Eritrean border town. Central Axis. Ethiopian federal and TPLF forces reportedly clashed in the mountainous Tigray interior south of Axum. Major Domestic Political Developments. The interim Tigray regional government has continued setting up its administration amid internal tensions. Ethiopian security forces are reportedly conducting forced conscription in the Oromia region and Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital. Regional and International Activity. Various international actors affirmed their support for de-escalation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, although officials from the two countries have continued to accuse each other of escalation. Figure 1. ENDF and TPLF Battle Across Tigray Note: ENDF stands for Ethiopian National Defense Force. TPLF stands for Tigray People’s Liberation Front. Source: Michael DeAngelo; Liam Karr; Alexander Brown. Eastern Axis: Afar Region Nothing significant to report. Northern Axis: Rama-Zalambessa-Dallol Local sources claimed that Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) fighters fought alongside the Tigray Defense Force (TDF), the TPLF’s military wing, against Ethiopian federal forces near the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, although CTP could not confirm the unverified claims. Federal and TDF forces reportedly clashed around Rama, which is approximately 20 miles north of Adwa and just south of the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, on November 7. [1] Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) reported that federal forces retook Rama, while the TDF claimed to have overcome federal forces and inflicted mass casualties upon them. [2] Fighting between the two sides reportedly broke out again around Rama between November 9 and 11. [3] The Ethiopian news outlet Wazema Radio cited residents who claimed that the AFNM and Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front—both of whom are members of the Alliance for Survival rebel coalition with the TPLF—fought alongside the TDF. [4] Conflict tracker Sajid Nadeem and another conflict tracker on X also reported that the AFNM participated in the fighting, although CTP could not confirm the unverified claims. [5] Western Axis: Humera-Addi Remets-Shire The Ethiopian military (Ethiopian National Defense Force, ENDF) reportedly sustained fighting with TDF and Eritrean forces around Badme, an Eritrean border town. The ENDF reportedly began fighting with TDF and Eritrean forces around the town on November 9 following several days of mutual buildups, although CTP could not verify whether fighting occurred on the Ethiopian or Eritrean side of the border. [6] Wazema Radio and a conflict tracker on X reported that the ENDF and TDF continued clashing on November 10 near Gomahalo, which is an Ethiopian village approximately 20 miles south of Badme. [7] The ENDF and Eritrean military (Eritrean Defense Forces, EDF) reportedly traded artillery fire around Badme from November 11 to 13. [8] The EDNF also reportedly conducted drone strikes on EDF positions. [9] The Ethiopian Conflict Map and Sajid Nadeem claimed that the ENDF captured Badme on November 12, although ACLED reported on November 13 that neither the ENDF nor the EDF controlled the town but that “Eritrean intelligence personnel” had been present. [10] The Ethiopian news outlet Addis Standard cited a resident of Badme who said that ENDF forces have been present in Badme since November 12, however. [11] Central Axis: Abiy Addi-Adwa-Axum Ethiopian federal forces and the TDF reportedly clashed in the mountainous Tigray interior south of Axum. The TDF has contested Ethiopian federal efforts to control areas around Tigray’s city belt since mid-October 2026. [12] The Ethiopian Conflict Map and Sajid Nadeem reported that the two sides clashed near Semema, which is approximately 20 miles south of Axum, on November 11. [13] Southern Axis: Mekele-Alamata-Sekota-Woldia Nothing significant to report. Northern Amhara Sector: From B21 Northward Nothing significant to report. Other Rebel Kinetic Activity Nothing significant to report. Major Domestic Political Developments The interim Tigray regional government has continued setting up its administration amid internal tensions. The interim administration has reportedly faced discord over appointments and governance, including payment of civil servants’ salaries. [14] A conflict tracker on X reported on November 11 that 11 senior members of Ethiopian Prime Ministerial Adviser Getachew Reda’s Simret party, which heavily influences the interim administration, resigned due to the discord. [15] Two conflict trackers separately reported on November 10 that the interim administration appointed Daniel Negash as “coordinator” for the Western Zone, which is disputed by Amhara and Tigrayan communities. [16] Ethiopian security forces are reportedly conducting forced conscription in the Oromia region and Addis Ababa. The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission and Addis Standard previously reported on forced conscription in Oromia in at least December 2024 and August 2026, respectively. [17] Addis Standard and the Canadian news outlet The Globe and Mail cited residents of Oromia and Addis Ababa on November 12 who reported that Ethiopian security forces had forcibly conscripted some of their family members and other civilians. [18] The Globe and Mail cited two residents of Addis Ababa who separately reported that the ENDF had sent their sons to the front lines in Tigray. [19] Addis Standard cited residents of Jimma, one of the largest cities in Oromia, who described forced conscription as a factor that sparked protests against regional and federal authorities on November 9 and 10. [20] Regional and International Activity Various international actors affirmed their support for de-escalation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, although officials from the two countries have continued to accuse each other of escalation. Five Democratic members of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee sent a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on November 10 that urged Rubio to increase US efforts to mediate between Ethiopia, Ethiopian rebel groups, and Eritrea. [21] The Democratic senators requested that the US State Department avoid offering Eritrea’s port of Assab to Ethiopia in any mediation and discourage Egypt, Eritrea, and Sudan from supporting Ethiopian rebel groups. [22] The Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers separately released a statement on November 11 after meeting in Paris that expressed “great concern” over tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea and called for “maximum restraint” and “diplomatic solutions.” [23] Special Envoy of the United Nations (UN) Secretary-General for the Horn of Africa Guang Cong met with Getachew on November 11 to discuss the security situation in the Horn of Africa. Cong has previously pledged that the UN will work toward peace and stability in the region. [24] Ethiopian and Eritrean officials have continued to accuse each other of escalation, which has been a pattern since the renewed war in northern Ethiopia began in late September 2026. Getachew posted on X that he discussed the “destructive role the Regime in Asmara is playing in the region” during his meeting with Cong. [25] Getachew also directly accused Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and Sudanese Transitional Sovereignty Council President Abdel Fattah al Burhan of equipping, arming, and coordinating with Ethiopian rebel groups, including by helping them conduct drone attacks in Ethiopia. [26] Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel posted on X on November 11 that Ethiopia has a “regional” war agenda. [27] The Eritrean Ministry of Information published an editorial on November 12 that accused Ethiopia of invading Eritrea. The handover ceremony was held at the headquarters of Uganda's 45th Battalion in Embresso and was led by its commander, Col. Dr. Justus Musenene, representing the commander of the First Division, Brig. Gen. Jackson Kayanja.
